The President is confident that the policy of broader and closer commercial relations with Canada will receive the hearty support of the large majority of the people of the United States, and he has learned with much satisfaction of the existence of a similar sentiment in the Dominion. It may be added that the conditions of the present day, as contrasted with the traditions of the past, are bringing into clearer light the truth that not only mutual trade interests but ethical and social considerations of the highest moment reinforce this common sentiment.
Let me, then, take this opportunity to express, by his direction, the desire of the President that your government will find it convenient to take up with this government, at such time and in such manner as may be mutually satisfactory, the consideration of a readjustment of our trade relations upon the broader and more liberal lines which should obtain between countries so closely related geographically and racially, as indicated by the President in his recent public utterances. I am, my dear Mr. Minister,
Very truly yours,
(Sgd.) P. C. KNOX. The Honourable W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance of the Dominion of Canada.
The other letter which concludes the correspondence is as follows:
Washington, March 26, 1910.
My dear Mr. Secretary,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of this date.
The Canadian government very heartily reciprocate your expressions as to the desirability of improving the commercial relations between the United States and Canada, and will gladly avail themselves of the invitation of the Presiden to take up with your government, at such time and in such manner as may bo mutually satisfactory, the consideration of a readjustment of these relations upon broad and liberal lines. The recent public utterances of the President in that direction have afforded much satisfaction to the Canadian people, who will receive with pleasure the formal confirmation of them, which is now conveyed to our government through you. I am confident that your assurances will be received also with much gratification by His Majesty's government in London, who will find in them further evidence of the desire of the government of the United States to maintain the most cordial relations with the British empire.
Allow me to express for myself as well as for my colleague, Mr. Graham, who has been associated with me in the conference at Washington, the most sincere thanks to the President and yourself for the cordiality of your welcome, and the very frank manner in which you have, discussed^ the questions that have engaged our attention.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) W. S. FIELDING. The Honourable P. C. Knox,
Secretary of State,
Washington.
I shall, Mr. Speaker, place upon the table for consideration in Committee of the

Whole, resolutions destined to give effect to the tariff changes -which I have already proposed to the House. I venture to present this statement, Sir, in the fullest confidence that it will commend itself to the judgment of the House-I trust I may say to both sides of the House, for there is and there should be no party question in such a matter. I am inclined to think that if we desired some momentarv\ popularity we might have pursued another course. I think there is a general and perhaps a justifiable feeling in the minds of the people of Canada, that in the years that have passed our American friends have not treated us generously or fairly with regard to these commercial questions, and consequently there is a strong disposition -at all events there has been a strong disposition-rather to resent any further communication with them. But, that is of a time that has gone; that is of a time when Ottawa went to Washington: Now we have reached a time when Washington has come to Ottawa, and that, I think1 Sir, is a matter which must be a source of gratification to us all. And though for the moment, by what is called the 'stand-pat' policy, by refusing to do anything, by bidding defiance to the United States, there might be a momentary hurrah, I am persuaded) that as the difficulties of the maximum tariff would become apparent, as great industries in Canada would be found to suffer, as men would find their capital impaired and as other men would find themselves thrown out of employment, even though it might be temporary, even though in the end we might have been able to overcome it : I am strongly persuaded that the feeling which at a moment might be one of gratification would change to a feeling of anxiety and alarm, and that in the end many a man would turn to the government and say: Was it not possible to have averted this disaster? was. it not possible by some moderate concession to have given the President of the United States an opportunity to pursue a more friendly course? And, if it could then be shown that some small and comparatively unimportant concessions could have effected a settlement, that the government could be rightfully charged to make these small concessions, that government would be condemned, and deservedly so. I present this question, Sir, with the fullest conviction that the small concessions we make are reasonable concessions for the purpose of meeting the United States- the President of the United States and -his Secretary of State particularly-in response to their good will. I accept the assurance of their good will for the present and of their good intentions for the future, and I am satisfied that in making this friendly
arrangement we are doing that which is best for the future of Canada.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
1 listened with a great deal of interest to the deliverance of the hon. the Finance Minister this afternoon, and propose to discuss it just a few moments. But, in the first place, I think the most important announcement made was that of the right hon. the First Minister that the Canadian government have agreed to exchange ratifications with regard to the International Waterways Commission. That is a very important measure, with far reaching consequences, involving in the highest degree very important interests to this country, and I hope that the treaty will have the effect of settling these international difficulties, and that the result will be beneficial to both countries. Any one who has followed the discussions in the United States recently must have remarked that Senator Root, who was Secretary of State in the late government, said that tariff complications were to be avoided above all things, because they might prevent the exchange of ratifications with regard to the waterways treaty. So that what we have had in this House to-day is the announcement of the settlement of two very important questions. One is the ratification of a treaty which will have the result of settling questions that arise with regard to waterways, and the other is the announcement of the Minister of Finance, that we have succeeded in avoiding a tariff war. That is a satisfactory, hut only temporary settlement of the situation. It is something like the feat of the King of France who marched up the hill with ten thousand men, and then marched them down again. However, there has been some kind of a settlement, and a better approach between the two nations has been reached, and to that extent I am glad to give the government credit for what they have done in the matter. The net result to my mind is this, that at last the great United States have been compelled to recognize that Canada is a free and independent nation on this great North American continent, and that we own, as I think, the better half of it. They have had to recognize also this fact that Canada is not only a free and independent nation, but that we are free to make our own tariff to suit ourselves, and to maintain our commercial autonomy in every sense of the term. The United States have been forced to recognize that, and it has taken a long while to bring that about. They have also been forced to recognize the right of Canada, net only to
make her own tariff for the benefit of her own people, and industries, but to give a preference to the mother country, and the associated states of the empire, and they also have been compelled to recognize our right to make reciprocal treaties with other nations throughout the world. There is also the recognition of the fact that Canada has the right to impose export duties^ Commercial independence, tariff independence, is largely brought about by export duties, and the resources winch ~ are contained in a protective tariff. It was a question of dispute in this country that a tariff could not be used to advance a country. We have demonstrated that it can. Sir John Macdonald, and those who were with him in the early days, and who inaugurated the National Policy, have been vindicated, and the position they took has been amply demonstrated, that a tariff, that bounties and export duties and that all the resources which are in the quiver of the protectionist, are available, and are necessary for the working out of the tariff independence of any nation. And that policy which was begun here a good many years ago with some trepidation, and for which failure was predicted, is to-day vindicated, and is to-day the greatest factor in building up this Canadian nation. Germany has had to recognize, the United States have had to recognize, that Canada is a vast country with a nationality, a fertility, and resources that must command the respect of all the nations of the world.
There is also in this situation a great lesson to the mother country. Our mother country, for some reason or other, and the public men of that country, for a great many years, have been led away by the doctrine that free trade was the best trade for England with other nations. The in-effitjacy of that doctrine has been proved now, and in no case has it been proved so pointedly as in this that Canada, by reason of her tariff position, can command just treatment from the United States which a country that has no tariff or no arrows in her quiver cannot command. If there be one searching thought in the minds of Englishmen to-day, it is that they have made the mistake of their life in thinking that free trade could enable them to get fair treatment from other nations. There is a great party growing up in England to-day which sees that a protective tariff, and even export duties are the only means by which they can compel other nations to treat England in a fairer way. So that the net profit to-day for the Canadian people is that the National Policy, which was started years ago, has vindicated itself, has been accepted by the people of this country, including hon. gentlemen opposite, and is capable of being used to obtain for us rights which we otherwise could not gain. But we must not be led away by

that very sweet letter of Secretary Knox which the Finance Minister read this afternoon with such gusto. The only time when the hon. gentleman becomes really effective is when that crescendo comes into his voice, and he becomes pathetic, as he certainly did this afternoon when he read that letter. But there is nothing in that letter. If you wish to gauge the friendliness of the United States you must examine its purpose, and not the letter of its diplomatists.	.
The tariff of the United States to-day is very unfriendly so far as we are concerned. But it is inspired-and we cannot blame the Americans for it-by the highest kind of national policy. It is designed for the protection of American industry. With that view, they have put their tariff in its most hostile attitude in regard to the products of Canada, that American tariff is a menace to Canada-hardly so designed, I would say-the object being the development of American industry, and it has succeeded most surprisingly in that respect. So, what I warn the House and the country of is this: We have had a friendly settlement of a question which might have involved a tariff war, but nothing has been done, as yet, to take out the sting that is in the American tariff for Canadian products, that seek the American market, and so our duty to-day is to continue in that national policy which is vindicated here today; not to begin to abandon it, or to think that the statement of Secretary Knox that he thinks highly of this country and of Canadian statesmen, can make up for any real disadvantages. The Americans still have their tariff in existence, and they intend to keep it there. And now, under our success of to-day-if it is a success, and I am willing to admit that it is-our duty is all the more the maintenance of a Canadian national policy and a Canadian tariff to meet the unfair tariff that the Americans now impose upon us. If the right to impose an export duty upon pulp has helped to bring this about, why should we not have an export duty upon pulp and other things as well?-on lumber, nickel, asbestos and other products of Canada that are not produced in any other country, and that are now sent out of Canada to the United States to make work for American workmen, profit for American capital and national prestige for the American people. The National Policy has succeeded so well that what we want now is to carry it further and use the instruments we have in our hands to bring the American nation to a sense of the fact that we are determined to go on with the building up of our nationality and the development of our resources.
And now I come to a question which is before this House in another form, but which must be settled. We can no longer Mr. W. F. MACLEAN
afford to allow Americans to come into our country and acquire franchises, to dam our rivers, and to export the power thus produced from Canadian waters to help in the development of the industries of the United States. The moment we let them see, not only that they cannot have our pulp, but that they cannot have our power, they will come to Ottawa again and make concessions, if they have not made them to-day, and make them in the way we want them-in the tariff they impose on the products of this country. We can compel our cousins and brothers in the United States to come to us and help us to develop our resources. There are two ways for the Americans to take part in the exploitation of Canada's resources. One is to come here with their capital and build up industries in Canada; the other is to take the products of Canada and ship them across the line for the development of the United States. We can compel the Americans to come here with their brains and capital and develop Canada's resources within our own territory. And that which enables us to do this is the right we have vindicated to-day, the right to impose export duties, the right to make our own tariff, and give preferences. So, while we should always be friendly with Washington, we should be prepared to carry out the policy that would force them to recognize the position of this country, will force them to come here and develop Canada's resources. No more must this idea be held of allowing them to raid our markets or to use our resources for their own benefit. If we carry out this idea, perhaps, some day, the Americans will come to us with some kind of trade reciprocity. They may say : we want your farm products, and we will remove some of the duties that we impose upon you. If they ever do come, it will be because Canada has taken the strong position of National Policy and is prepared to maintain her commercial integrity no matter at what cost. We must be careful not to be so anxious to win sweet words from the Americans that we shall in any way jeopardize the early carrying out of what I believe is in the air-preferential trade within the empire. I believe there is more for Canada, in her present situation and in her future, in closer relations with the mother country, and with the sister states of the empire than in closer trade relations with the United States. Anything we get from the United States will be the result of-I must use the word, for it is the only one that applies-the result of retaliation. It was this that brought them to time today-not sweet words, but the fact that we have the instruments of retaliation in our hands. As between Canada and the mother country, and between Canada and the sister states of the empire, there is a friendly feeling; there is the knowledge

that we are bound together now by ties ot defence. We must be careful now, in any negotiations we carry on, not to prejudice our chances of greater reciprocal trade within the empire. The one thing that brought the Americans to time to-day was not even the fear of retaliation from Canada or the danger to the republican party of the United States if they imposed the maximum tariff against this country, as the fear that has got into the American mind that the British empire is getting together with regard to trade, and they would like to forestall that coming together if they could.
So we need not fear, from this time, that the Americans will take the attitude they once took with regard to us of refusing to deal with us, and, when we asked them, sending us home with an admonition to mind our own business. They see that Canada has vindicated her tariff integrity, and that Canada, and the empire are coming together for the development of some kind of inter-imperial preferential trade. That being the case I say that the position of Canada is a magnificent one. It is no more surrender or give away. We have now simply got to sit tight, not to sit pat, but sit tight on the policy of the development of our own resources in every direction, to keep all Canadian work for Canadian workingmen, to keep the raw products of Canada within the boundaries of Canada for their subsequent manufacture, and if we find unfair treatment meted out to us by any nation, not to be afraid to apply the lex talionis with regard to that nation. An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, is still good law in tariff situations. It has .been effective in the past, it is effective to-day, and it will be effective in the future. To my mind, as I have said, the net result of the negotiations closed to-day is that Canada has vindicated her position, not only territorially, but she has vindicated her tariff integrity. She has shown her ability to take care of herself, and to join up with the empire in making the empire greater, and in drawing all portions of the empire closer together. She has established the fact that the only instrument towards achieving national greatness, towards achieving imperial greatness, towards compelling respect from all other nations, is the adoption of a tariff policy, and the use of that tariff instrument will compel the recognition of all these things by outside nations. Therefore, what the government has done today in bringing about the recognition that tariff war is not a good thing for either country, they are entitled to what credit they can get out of it. The Canadian people will also be ready to say to-day that the National Policy on which thi3 country embarked some years ago with so much fear and trepidation has more than justified itself, because it has to-day become the basis of Canadian nationality, and of any greatness that Canada may attain on this continent.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Maclean) ha3 called attention to the fact that to-day marks a notable point in the history of the development of this country. He says that we have to-day exemplified in a very vivid manner that this country has a perfect right to make its own treaties, that it is independent in tariff matters, and that foreign countries have to come to us if they want to make treaties with us. I had always understood that this country was a free democracy-of course under the British Crown. From away back since confederation, the doctrine has never been questioned that we have a perfect right to make our own tariffs. In regard also to making our own treaties, it was not a question of wrenching any right or prerogative whatsoever from the British Crown; it was simply a matter for us to say whether we desired the right to make our own treaties. No limit has ever been placed upon our freedom to do what we pleased in this respect, except the limit that has been placed by the constitution drafted by the people of this country themselves. For that reason I do not see that there is any credit pertaining to the government of the day in effecting this treaty. This is no fresh victory for liberty, because we have just as great liberty as any other portion of the empire. But there seems to be an under current flowing through the speeches of hon. members, particularly on the other side of the House, to the effect that there is a struggle for liberty constantly going on between this country and the mother country, a struggle to acquire some constitutional right. I fail to see it, and no one who is a student of history but must recognize the folly and childishness of anybody who makes that remark.
The Minister of Finance has placed before the House to-day some facts with reference to the treaty, or the alleged treaty, of reciprocity, or whatever you might call it, between this country and the United States. Hj laboured for two hours to make his meaning clear, although I am free to admit that he was sometimes interrupted. But after hearing what he had to tell the House, I thought that at the tail end of his speech he was very much like the man who for a bet rolls a pea uft and down the sidewalk with a toothpick. The whole object of his speech was to show that Canada had made certain concessions to the United States on 13 items, which, after all, did not amount to anything to speak of, end I thought that if be required

two hours to speak of these 13 items, how long wmuld he have required to speak if he had talked of every item in the tariff.
Now, let me take up the real question at issue in this matter. It was not a question at all of whether we1 should give any treaty rights to the Americans, or anything of that kind, as regards any item in the tariff. The issue was simply and plainly this: Have the Americans the right to dominate this country and say to us: Unless you do so and so we will be unfriendly to you. That to my mind is the whole question at issue in this matter. This country was not the country that brought about this condition. We had nothing to do with the framing of this Payne tariff, we made no promises, we were dealing peaceably with the facts as they existed, carrying on our own business, doing our own work, getting our three meals a day, living peaceably with everybody else in the world. Now, what more? The United States of America which has always stood ouc against this two columned tariff which they have recently adopted, finds that the markets of the world are gradually being closed against it. They found France closed against them, they found Spain closed against them, they found Italy closing its doors against them, they found that Germany had closed, its doors against them, and there was no door left open to them but that of Great Britain. So they spy: We will construct this two column tariff and with it we will force Germany, France and Canada to open their markets to us. Now, they passed this Payne-Aldrich tariff, as they call it, and what has happened? This country has been the only country in the world that has surrendered to that Payne tariff that has yielded to the threat of that club. Has Germany surrendered one particle, or France either? They can go on doing business at the old stand in whatever way they like. But we cannot. The way this treaty reads we have surrendered our rights to make our own tariff, we make this maximum and minimum tariff, once you have established a tariff by treaty you cannot raise that tariff. The Minister of Finance is not present but I ask the leader of the government, is it not a fact that once you make a treaty with a country and you fix a rate at a certain figure you surrender your right ever afterwards to change that rate unless you reduce it or denounce the treaty. Of course, he knows very well that is so. They have surrendered now on 13 items, and the next year the United States will come up with some more legislation and clubs and we will have to surrender on twice 13 items. The next year . after they will introduce some more club legislation and we will have to surrender on 50 items, and they will continue slaughtering us in that way. We have let1

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
the opportunity go by. For once in the history of this country we find ourselves in a position to dictate terms to them, and what have we received? Have wre received a single concession beyond what we have had before? We have received nothing but the promise of a president. How many times has a president of the United States promised this country reciprocity of concessions? Time and again, five or six times. Not only that, but five or six times they have sent treaties to Congress giving concessions to this country only to find the treaties kicked out.
Now this is not a matter of our making conditions with the United States. We have surrendered. We have entered the thin edge of the wedge on the question of surrendering to the United States of the right to interfere with our constitutional rights to make our own tariff, and the business people of this country and those who know anything about tariff matters will not overlook that very important point. Let us go back over this very important question. The minister know's that that treaty was aimed at two countries particularly-Germany and Canada. I was very much amused to see the discussion in the Liberal papers about this matter leading to reciprocity. Anybody who knows anything about treaties or treaty-making knows very well that the idea of a reciprocity treaty does not exist to-day as it did before 1890i. The whole form of making commercial treaties has changed, and there is no countries in the world, except the United States and Great Britain, which clings to the old reciprocity treaty idea. Anybody knows that by making this double column tariff, as they have done recently, the United States have also given up the idea of a reciprocity treaty. What is the difference between a reciprocity treaty so-called and a favoured-nation clause treaty? A reciprocity treaty is a straight treaty between two countries in which one country says: We will admit certain articles free, or under, certain conditions, into our country if you will admit certain articles under similar conditions into yours, and it is a bargain between the two of us. That was the kind1 of treaty we negotiated in 1854, but that kind of treaty-making has gone out of fashion.! They talk about obtaining commercial treaties on a reciprocal basis with the United States. Why, there are fourteen of these reciprocal treaties with foreign countries hung up which never have passed Congress. The treaties that are now passed' are such as we have made with France, containing a favoured-nation clause. The favoured-nation clause has been very dangerous to us, and is the thing that has brought us into this trouble. When you make a treaty with any country, which treaty contains a favoured-nation clause, every other country having a treaty with1

the country with which you are dealing is entitled to similar concessions, and it obtains those concessions without giving anything in return for them. You piay give great concessions to France in order to make a treaty, but you must give the benefits of that treaty to every country in the union of favoured nations, without perhaps any return. Supposing Canada made a reciprocal treaty with the United States, every privilege given to the United States must automatically go to France. That is the condition and that is the reason why the Minister of Finance has placed these items in such a way that they are, open to, every country in the world, so that he would not have to acknowledge to thisi House that he had made such a fool treaty as the French treaty is. Let us glance briefly over this matter of treaty making between Canada and the United States. It Was in 1846 that the question first came up. A form of treaty was then negotiated, but it came to naught. Finally, after a great deal of trouble, a treaty was passed in 1854, and it continued from 1854 until 1865. That treaty was of great benefit to this country. Anybody who studies the statistics of that period will know that our trade with the United States was speedily placed upon an even basis. When the treaty was made, the United States sold to Canada $24,000,000 worth of goods, while Canada sold to the United States $8,000,000 worth. In 1865, when the treaty was denounced, Canada bought from the United States $27,000,000 worth of goods and sold them $33,000,000. The reason why that treaty was denounced was that the Americans claimed that this country was making a tariff which would operate, against American manufacturers, and they claimed that we were violating the treaty in spirit. They saw a few factories growing up in this country. Canada had adopted a certain amount of protection, and some factories were built. When the Americans saw factories going up, even saw-mills, they got angry and' said: We will denounce that treaty, or you will have to stop building factories over in Canada. Everybody knows that these charges were made in 'Congress and in the public press, and that these are the true reasons for the abrogation of that treaty* Since then we have made, various efforts to negotiate a treaty with the United States. As the Minister of Finance said, the Hon. George Brown went to Washington and negotiated a treaty. Anybody who reads the life of George Brown knows thatt John Sandfield Macdonald, at the time the leciprocity treaty was denounced, asked the editor of the ' Globe ' to go to Washington as a quasi representative of the Canadian! government to negotiate a treaty on the quiet, exactly as his follower to-day has done. The correspondence is published in tlie ' Life of George Brown/ by Alexander Mackenzie, and no doubt the able editor of the ' Globe ' is a careful student of the life of his predecessor and has followed the same course. In 1874, a new treaty was negotiated. It was adopted by the President of the United States and by this government, and it was a very good treaty. But as soon as it went to Congress it was thrown out because the United States said that if they could squeeze Canada against the wall, she would very soon come into the union. That process, then adopted, has been going on, the United States government has been holding a club over us, and the imposition of a surtax is only another effort to club us into submission. With all due respect to the story that the Finance Minister has put up that this is a great and notable victory for us? the truth is that we have surrendered, that we have shown the white flag. What was done? The United States sell to Canada vast quantities of goods, the principal articles being manufactures of iron and steel. The right hon. First Minister has just withdrawn the surtax against Germany. Germany is a great producer of iron and steel, and as a purchaser of steel, I can assure you that steel can be bought cheaper in Germany than in the United States. There i3 not a single article on the iron and steel schedule to-day but what can be purchased as cheaply outside of the United States as in the United States, if not more cheaply. The other large export from the United States to Canada is farm products. There is not a single thing in the whole category of these farm products that is not manufactured by the farmers of this country. I say manufactured, because I believe that the farmers are the biggest manufacturers in Canada, they are using more machinery and employing a greater number of men than all other manufacturers. There is not an article in that schedule but what could and should be produced in this country. One article on that schedule is coal. Coal is dutiable, and no country would derive greater benefit from a reciprocal treaty with regard to coal than the United States would. The coal fields of the United States are in the Pennsylvania valley, and they can supply coal to the province of Ontario. A few years ago the province of Ontario would require an immense amount of coal in order to turn the wheels of the factories. But, thanks to Sir James Whitney and his progressive policy which is resulting in the development of the water-powers of that province, in a few years there will not be such a thing as a coal-driven power plant in Ontario. It is said that the United States might prohibit the sending of coal into this country, but the fact is that the New England states must have Canadian coal, and they are obliged to pay for it a higher price than I as a consumer of coal would like to have to pay. The millions of

tons of coal produced in the Crowsnest pass go chiefly to the United States, as is also the case with the millions of tons produced at Nanaimo, and, therefore, reciprocity in coal would not affect us to any appreciable extent. In fact, Sir, I believe it would benefit our country. It seems strange to me, and to other users of coal all oveif Canada, why, when the Minister of Finance had an opportunity of doing a little trick by giving reciprocity in something, he did not give reciprocity in soft coal. We all know that the duty on coal is higher than the duty on any other single article in this country, because the cost of coal at the pit mouth in Pennsylvania never exceeds $1 a ton, and the duty is over 50 cents a ton. I do not think that the Cape Breton coal fields would lose anything by reciprocity in coal, because I am satisfied that the miners in Nova Scotia would give up the Montreal market to-morrow if they were able to enter the New England and New York markets.

speechtext:
Yes, and the reason is that the market of eastern Canada is restricted for Nova Scotia coal, whereas the market in New England and the eastern states is almost unlimited if there was'reciprocity. I am surprised that the Minister of Finance with his free trade ideas, did not give reciprocity on a few of the agricultural implement schedules. There is no doubt in the world that the great trusts in the United States were moving heaven and earth to prevent a tariff wan We buy $20 per capita to the $1 per capita the Americans buy from us. The leather trust, that has a little edge in! here to-day they did not want a tariff war; the glass trust, one of the largest trusts in the United States which controls the machinery for making common glass holds the trade of the United States to-day and they did not want any tariff war with Canada. Then, there is the crockery trust which wants privileges in Canada and they did not want any higher duty placed against them in the Canadian market. To m.y mind one of the principal objections to a reciprocity treaty with the United States is that the people of Canada suffer enough to-day from local and small trusts without being inundated by the huge American trusts, which would be the result if we enter into reciprocity with them. Almost everything to-day in the United States is in the hands of a trust. Only recently in this parliament we had in evidence the United States water-power trust putting up a fight and we could see how long their arm is. There is a trust on everything in the United States except air, and I have no doubt that when airships become popular they will have the heavens chartered and they Mr J. A. CURRIE.
will be selling us the atmosphere. It is quite possible that in a few years, the member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee)-I am sorry he is not here to-night-will be seeking a charter for a company to navigate the air for the general advantage of Canada, and when they have got that 'general advantage of Canada' clause in their charter they will make us all pay so much per cubic foot for the air we breathe. Hon. gentlemen may talk about reciprocity in products in any shape or form, but there is nothing to be gained for Canada in that. I need not remind the House that the United States has been hostile to this country in tariff matters from time immemorial. No move has ever been made in this country to get any advantage in trade or navigation that the United States did not do all they could to hamper us and to harm us. Look at what was done in the case of the St, Mary's canal. An effort was made to take the duty off ships going through the Canadian canals in order to increase our lake tonnage, but to counteract this move an Act of Congress was passed by which they shut Canadian vessels out of that canal, and they compelled Canada to go to an expense of $5,000,000 to build a special lock at Sault Ste. Marie. I grant you that the items mentioned by the Minister of Finance amount to nothing, but he has done a great injury to Canada in that he has acknowledged that the United States can get an act of Congress passed and hold a club over the head of the people of this country which they will threaten to use on us unless we bow the knee to them. I think, Sir, the people of Canada have reached the belief that the sooner we light fire with fire and tariff with tariff the better for us. Then, the Americans will come not to Albany but to Ottawa. True, they sent a few young men up here, but the big men only came as far as Albany and the Minister of Finance went to meet them there. I want to tell vou that all the circumstances surrounding this matter appear very strange to me. Who was the editor of the Toronto ' Globe ' working for in the matter; who was he saving the money for? It is worth millions to the American steel trust and the other American trusts to be able to market their goods in Canada. The American steel trust sends some $60,000,000 worth of goods to Canada, and here we have a Canadian going to Albany and doing the lobbying for them. And when we all thought that possibly there might be a little fight, and having gone through a small fight with Germany from which no Canadian suffered, and Germany having thrown up the sponge, then, in the moment of victory the Minister of Finance is called in haste to an interview with the President of the United States, and when he emerges from

his interview he has bowed the knee to Baal and acknowledged that Canada is subject to the United States. I think the people of Canada will recognize that whether there is a large concession or a small concession given to the United States we have abnegated the great principle that we are competent to make tariffs to suit ourselves, and that no country in the world can hold a club over us whether it be the United States or Germany or any other nation. That is the proper principle for us to maintain, that is the principle we should have maintained, but we have lost prestige in this transaction, and the man I blame for it most of all is the Prime Minister of Canada who doubtless instigated the visit of the Finance Minister to Washington.
I hope he will frankly and truthfully tell the House whether Mr. Macdonald was accredited by him to go down and endeavour to patch up some kind of peace with Secretary Knox and the president. If he was not, why then should any attention have been paid to Mr. Macdonald? Why was there such hot haste, why were there telegrams and sudden visits to Albany by the minister and a treaty patched up? What for? Not to give anything to Canada, because we have always had the same thing and we were certainly entitled to every privilege from the United States, we were their best customers, but in order that something might be done, which, to my mind, was derogatory to the principles of fair play and Canadianism which every Canadian in this country wishes to stand up for. The Prime Minister has told us time and again that we do not want any trade with England. Everybody knows that if Great Britain should give us a preference of say a shilling a quarter on wheat it would mean millions to the farmers of this country. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have said that we do not want anything of the kind, we do not want any concessions of any kind from Great Britain. Yet he will go to Albany and bow the knee to get concessions from the President of the United States.
These thoughts that I have briefly and crudely placed before the House are thoughts that occur to the ordinary individual of this country. The people of Canada have come to the conclusion that as far as any business relations with the United States are concerned, the government of the day are not to be trusted because the interests of this country will suffer in their hands and will be given away.

ARMSTRONG (East Lambton) Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) must have been very much encouraged by the remarks of the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). I would suggest that he should get a nice soft seat for him over on that
side and take good care of him as I under stand his paper is owned and controlled by the government of the country, or at least by some one very close to the government. Be that as it may, the Finance Minister this afternoon tried to make this House and the people of this country believe that as far as the present trade arrangement was concerned, he had received from the United States some valuable consideration for the people of this country That hon. gentleman knows full well that instead of receiving any consideration from the government of the United States he was only too ready and willing to get down on his knees practically speaking and beg and plead that the government of the United States would accept as small concessions as possible in order that he might get out of the position he was in. He knows that the exercise of treaty making powers by him in years gone by has not resulted greatly to his interest. If he considers the treaty arrangement with Germany he cannot but appreciate that instead of our having access to the German markets for all the products of our country we have access to that country for only a very small proportion of our products while on the other hand the German people have access to our markets for all the products of Germany on the very same footing they had in 1896. We have access to the German markets for only a very small proportion of the products of Canada. Then, let him consider the French treaty. I was one of those who opposed it as strongly as possible, condemned it in every way and voted in direct opposition to it, believing and knowing that it would be of no benefit to Canada while we were granting valuable concessions to France. Not only were we granting these concessions but we were paying some $200,000 per annum in subsidies to steamships that could only be carrying some of the products of the manufacturers of Canada, while the Finance Minister knows that French products have been coming into this country in increased proportions, while we were unable to get our products into France in return. That French treaty, as he had to admit to-day, was the cause of all the trouble with the United States. He knows that when this matter was up for discussion he gave the members on this side to understand that the French treaty would not be interfered with in any way by the people of the United States. Yet we find him in the very position that we pointed out he would be in only a few months ago. When the Finance Minister tries to make us believe that he has obtained concessions from the United States., he knows that instead of obtaining concessions, he was only too ready and willing to give them what they have to-day. Let us see for a moment the position that we are in in regard to.

speechtext:
Every tariff since 1890, except the Wilson Act (and even that in certain particulars), has made it harder for Canada to do any business in the United States. The trade in barley was slaughtered, the wheat business was cut to the lowest level, the tariff on paper was kept at tremendous height. Whenever Canada thought she saw a chance to build up a trade in the United States, the next tariff Act regularly cut off the possibility.
I could go on reading paper after paper of the United States going to show that'' they are more than delighted with the outcome of the treaty arrangement with Canada. They emphatically state that it would be impossible for the President of the United States to force through such a measure as our Finance Minister seems to think he would. Canada has certainly suffered humiliation at the hands of this government, especially when we consider the fact that the government was backed up in a firm stand against any concessions by practically every newspaper in the Dominion, Liberal and Conservative, outside of perhaps the Toronto ' Globe.' On the 17th of March, the Toronto ' Globe ' made this statement:	%
The Liberals are firm. Prepared to face tariff war if necessary.
But on March 28, it took back practically all it had said. Would the hon. minister consider this fact, that we are buying from the United States $25 worth of goods for every man, woman and child in Canada, whereas the people of the United States buy from us only one dollar of goods for every man, woman, and child, in the United States. Then look at the message which President Taft sent to Congress when he said that the results of the meeting with the Canadian statesmen were satisfactory. The opposition voted against the French treaty. Are we as Canadians going to make a present of our trade advantages to every country which asks for it? You can depend upon it that if we continue the policy that we have laid down with regard to our trade relations, that, as years go by, we will have more and more complications in our tariff arrangements with other countries, and can expect to be placed in just such a humiliating position as we are placed in to-day; and I sincerely hope that whenever the opportunity comes the Finance Minister will arrive at some definite tariff arrangement whereby we shall have one maximum and one minimum rate for all countries. I merely rose to utter my protest against the present arrangement forced upon the Finance Minister, and I trust that in future, if he should take into consideration the tariff, and treaty arrangements of other foreign countries with Canada, he will also get closer to the question of how these arrangements

will affect our position from a British standpoint.

speechtext:
The thing is a slander, so far as the government is concerned, and a slander also so far as the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) is concerned. I think it is also to be regretted too that so much importance should be attached to the fact that Mr. Macdonald, the editor of the ' Globe/ went to the United States. My hon. friend beside me (Mr. Fielding) said in the course of his remarks that, after the matter had been brought to his attention again and again and he had treated it as a joke, he finally made it clear that Mr. _ Macdonald went to the United States on his own account, and never had a mission from this government. Yet although this was the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding), the hon. member for Simooe (Mr. Currie) put the question seriously whether or not Mr. Macdonald had been sent as an emissary or as a deputed agent by this government to the United States. I have only to reply that this government sent no ambassador to Washington. We received ambassadors from Washington. Things have been reversed, as has been said by my hon. colleague (Mr. Fielding). However, I pass by these matters, which have no reference to the question we have to deal with at present.
We had to deal with a question which was a very serious one because we were in this situation that we were threatened "with commercial war with our neighbours. And I have heard Sir Charles Tupper say years ago-and perhaps my hon. friends opposite may remember it-that 'commercial war was not far removed from actual war. It would be a calamity that between Canada and the United States, the United States would impose its maximum tariff upon Canada, and Canada treat the United States in like manner. Every body would regret it, and the action we took was with a view to avert such a calamity, I am 191
free to say that the United States, in the tariff they adopted at their last session of Congress, took a position which Canada would never agree to. The position taken by the United States, in their Act of Congress, was to this effect, that if any two other nations made a treaty of commerce between themselves, by which the one would exchange favours with the other, the United States had the right to ask from both the most favoured nation treatment, and if that were not done, they would impose their maximum tariff on the offending nation. If, for instance, Canada made a treaty with France, or Germany, or Italy, or Belgium, or any other nation, whereby Canada would exchange favours with that nation, the United States had the right to claim similar treatment, and if we refused they would impose on us their maximum "tariff. That matter came up in the early part of the session. After parliament met and the negotiations with France came up for discussion, we were asked "to ascertain what would be the attitude of the United States if our parliament were to ratify the treaty we had negotiated with France. We refused to consider that question. The position we took was that, having made a treaty with France, ve were bound in honour to call on parliament to ratify that treaty, and the United States had no business to interfere in our relations with any other country. We therefore refused to consider what would be the consequences of the ratification by parliament of the treaty we had negotiated with France. At the same time we had reason to believe that, although Congress had adopted the tariff they did and they did it with a great deal of hesitation- there was a large portion of public opinion in the United States which was adverse to the enforcement of the extreme measure put by Congress on its statute-books. We had reason to believe that a large portion of the American people would be sorry that there would be anything but the most friendly commercial relations with Canada, and the event has shown that our surmise was well founded, because when the time was approaching to put the maximum tariff in- operation-as the first of April was approaching-there was a strong feeling of _uneasiness in the United States lest the president would feel constrained to apply against Canada the maximum tariff. Indeed the feeling in the United States was such that, for the first time in the history of Canada, we had American commissioners sent by the government of Washington to negotiate with the Canadian government, and ascertain what would be our position.
Sir, the answer we had to give to the American commissioners was easy for us. We have been requested to place upon the



table the correspondence which embodied our answer to the question. There was no correspondence on this point. The answer we had to give was known by the House even before we uttered it. The answer we gave the American commissioners was the same as we have given to parliament-that the relations between Canada and France as embodied in that treaty had nothing to do with the United States, and the United States had nothing to do with them, and could not be concerned in them. True, the Americans might take a different position; they might say they were concerned in our relations with the other country and wanted to know what those relations were. Our answer would be: These relations, of course, are known; we have given France certain concessions in exchange for the preference she has given us; if you are prepared to give us the same treatment we are prepared to discuss the matter with you; if not, you have no questions to ask us. But it is well known that there was in the United States a different school of thought upon this question. I have stated that we had reason to believe that a very large proportion of American public opinion was averse to any estrangement in the relations between the United States and Canada. But we know very well that there is in the United States an extreme protectionist party which would push the president to apply the maximum tariff against Canada. We know also that there was a certain opinion in Congress and in the entourage of the president that, according to the terms of the law, the president would be bound to hold that the treaty we had made with France was an undue discrimination against the United States, and that, therefore, to put in force the maximum tariff. But, dominating all the situation, there was a strong proportion of public opinion-I believe a preponderating public opinion-which deprecated the possibility of the maximum tariff being put in force against Canada. We did not know exactly what would take place; we did not know whether the president would, or would not, feel himself constrained to put upon us the maximum tariff-there was the possibility. Will anybody refuse to approve my words when 1 say that if we could avoid the possibility of such a result without the sacrifice of Canadian dignity or interest, it was our duty to take the course which woul'd bring about that result? At any rate, I take the position in the name of the government and in the presence of the Canadian people, with regard to the United States and every other nation we will do everything possible to maintain in the case of one and all the best relations consistent with the maintenance of the dignity and the interest of Canada. It was represented to us that if Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
we would make certain concessions we should avoid the possibility of any difficulty with our neighbours, we should avoid the possibility of having this maximum tariff enforced against us. Very well, our answer was easy. We were asked: Cannot you make it easy for us, cannot you make some concessions? We asked: What are these concessions? We were told a moment ago by the? hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) that w*e had made a surrender. What have we surrendered? In this discussion with the United States representatives we were told: All difficulties will be overcome, all danger will be averted if you will give some concessions. We said: Very well, we will make concessions if it will make it easy for you to give Canada the benefit of the minimum tariff. We were asked: Can you make a concession on figs and dates? We thought that we could give figs and dates without making too great a sacrifice of Canadian dignity, of Canadian interests. Could we give prunes also? Well, we thought that the dignity of Canada would not be interfered with if we gave prunes. We were asked if we could concede also almonds, walnuts, Brazil nuts, pecans and shelled peanuts. Yes, we thought we could give peanuts also. And nuts of all kinds? Yes, and nuts of all kinds. Then, as to photographs, chromos chromotypes, artotypes, oleographs, paintings, drawings, pictures, decalcomania transfers of all kinds, engravings or Drints or proofs therefrom, and similar works of art not otherwise provided; blue-prints, building plans, maps and charts. We thought we could concede these also. We were asked if we could give soap powders, powdered soap and so on. Yes, we thought it was worth while to give even soap powders for the benefit of peace. Then, perfumery, including toilet preparations, non-alcoholic, namely, hair oils- we thought we could concede hair oils- tooth an 1 other powders and washes, pomatums, and so on.. Yes, we thought we could go that far; we surrendered that. Asked if we could give tableware of China, porcelain, white granite ana iron stone- things not manufactured in this country- we were prepared to concede that. And window glass? It is not manufactured in Canada; we conceded that. Watch actions and movements and parts thereof? Yes, we conceded that. Then there was leather-dongola, cordovan calf, sheep, lamb, kid or goat, kangaroo, alligator and all leather dressed, waxed, glazed or further finished than tanned. Yes, we gave that, as it is a raw material for our boot and shoe makers. And last, we were asked if we could give feathers and manufacture of feathers, imitations of fruit, grains, leaves and flowers suitable for ornamenting hats. These are to ornament the hats

of Canadian ladies. We conceded that also. These are the concessions we have made; these reductions of tariff are made not to the United States alone, but to the whole worid.
And now, I am asked: what do you get from these concessions? I answer: We get peace and good relations with our neighbour. And I ask hon. members on the other side: Is not peace and good commercial relations with our neighbours worth all the feathers and artificial flowers in creation? But we are told by my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie):	The Americans were bluffing; they
were not sincere. Perhaps they were bluffing, as the hon. member says. Or perhaps they were sincere. We were in this position, if we had been stiff with them, they might have chosen to be stiff with us. Canadians number seven millions, while Americans are ninety millions. We have surrendered nothing, we have made concessions which amount to nothing, so far as I can see; and for these we have the good will of that great nation. It is true, we have not reciprocity. My hon. friend from North Simcoe asked: Why did you not get reciprocity in coal, which is so much wanted in Ontario; why did you not get reciprocity in agricultural implements, which are needed in the Northwest provinces? This is true, and it is true also that wre are within measurable distance of obtaining a treaty of reciprocity with our neighbours. There is a possibility of settling all these questions without sacrificing anything. We are to-day in the same position we were three months ago. We have retained our absolute power and freedom of action. We can negotiate treaties with any nations we please, and we intend to do so by commencing with the United States. We can negotiate a treaty with Germany, we can negotiate a treaty with Italy, we can negotiate a treaty with Belgium. We are absolutely free, we have made no surrender of any right, and the first thing we shall do is to endeavour to negotiate with our neighbours, and if possible to get a treaty of commerce with them. We are not insensible to the suggestion of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), who advises us to go slowly in this matter. We do not intend to go very fast. There are certain things upon which we can make no concessions, there are certain duties upon which we can not recede one iota from our present position. But there are a number of products in regard to which it would be for the mutual advantage of Canada and the United States that there should be the widest possible extension of our markets on both sides of the line. This is the position we have taken up. I am a little astonished that my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) should not have given us the credit to which I think we are entitled. Now, I can 191J
not take my seat without taking advantage of this occasion to say that, although I have always btien proud of my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Finance, 1 was never so proud of him as I am to-day. It is due to his efforts that we have averted very serious trade complications with our neighbours. It is due to his efforts, to his conciliatory and clever methods, that we have obtained at last a better treaty of commerce with our neighbours.

speechtext: I rise to a question of privilege. I wish to say a few words on the resolution now before the House. Might I suggest to the Minister of Finance, now that lie has capitulated to the United States government, and while these tariff arrangements are under consideration, that this would be a splendid opportunity for him to do something for the western farmers. I think it would be a much greater benefit to this country to put binders on the free list than feathers or perfumery, and things like that of which we have heard to-night. I think this would have been a grand opportunity for the government to fulfil some of the pledges they made years, ago to the farmers of the Northwest. We' know that prior to 1896 the Prime Minister and his follows ers made pledges that if they were in power they would put farm implements on the free list. I do not know whether the Prime Minister himself made that statement emphatically, but many of his followers who afterwards became ministers did make it. I think this would have been a fitting opportunity to insist upon reciporcity in agricultural implements between the two ooun-Mr. SPEAKER.
tries as well as in wheat and other grains. The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. knowles) has had a resolution on the order paper asking for lower duties on farm implements for the benefit of the farmers. I think it is time we should try to do something for the farmers of the west. This resolution reads as follows.:-
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that the government should at an early date take into serious consideration the necessity for the reduction of the tariff duties of Canada

speechtext: I just want to say a few words upon this matter. The fact that these negotiations have been going on amused me very much. I Temem'ber that prior to 1896 the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his associates stated that when they got into power they would go to Washington and get a treaty; in fact, we would have free trade between the two countries. Shortly after they came into power in 1896 the Prime Minister did go to Washington and he knows the reception he got there. He could not do anything.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: They were put on the free list by the Prime Minister on this trip. After a number of years we find the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister again going to Washington. This time the Finance Minister says that he had the invitation of the president, but if we read between the lines in the Toronto 'Globe' we find that they invite the editor of the Toronto 'Globe' to Ottawa and that he gets instructions to go down to see President Taft and have President Taft send a telegram up inviting the Minister of Finance to a conference. The editor of the 'Globe' came to Ottawa after his interview in Washington. Every one around the House could see him in the lobbies talking with members and ministers and it was the gossip of the lobbies here that an arrangement had been made for the Minister of Finance to be telegraphed for to go down to Washington and interview the president. The interview was arranged in that way and the invitation came from President Taft. When the hon. Finance Minister went to Washington the first thing that he should have done was to try and do something in the interests of the farmers. We all know that the farming industry is the most important industry and the whole asset practically of the Dominion of Canada. But instead of that, when the Finance Minister gets down to Washington, he goes over the tariff to see what can be done to benefit Canada, and the first item that he takes is that of perfumery. He is''willing to allow perfumery to come in free. Then we find on the list feathers, nuts, raisins, &c. These are the things that he is looking after instead of doing something for the farmers. We were promised that when this government came into power in 1896 we would have agricultural implements coming into this country free, but there has been no reduction in the tariff with respect to these articles. The same tariff obtains now practically that was in existence in 1896. What surprises me is that the Minister of Finance did not try to negotiate a reciprocity in so far as agricultural implements are concerned. Then, there is wheat, the great output of the northwest. If we could get wheat into the United States it would be a great help to the farmers of the northwest. But the Minister of Finance did not take the farmers into consideration at all, in so far as the northwest was concerned, and did not try to get any of these articles on the free list.

speechtext:
It is a good thing to know that because it would be very serious if a verbal understanding of that kind were carried out. Another thing I fear may result from this arrangement is this:	The
very fact of this government having to agree to reduce the tariff, or make certain tariff changes, in order to satisfy the United States government makes me feel that if we were at any future time making treaties with other countries we would practically have to consult the United States, and make

the same arrangements with them. We are talking about making treaties with Italy, and other countries. What position are we in if we undertake to make a treaty with one of those countries? If we make a treaty with some other country will not the United States government apply this maximum tariff to Canada? Would it not have been well to have had it settled once and for all? I believe that had we stood in the position we were in prior to making this arrangement we would have been able to come to an understanding and probably we would have been able to make a treaty with the United States from which we would have benefited more than we can under the present arrangement. Our position now is that we are at the mercy of the United States in coming to any further trade relations with them. I believe the concessions we have given them will hamper us in the future in making a more beneficial arrangement. I move the adjournment of the debate.

speechtext: Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX (Postmaster General) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 104) to control the rates and facilities of ocean cable companies, and to amend the Railway Act with respect to telegraphs and telephones, and the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. He said: For many years the people of Ganada, and especially those connected with the press, have been trying to obtain lower rates from the cable companies. On several occasions the question was taken up, especially by my predecessor, Sir William Mulock, and also by a man who has taken a great interest in this matter, working, I believe, in the best interests of the country, Sir Sandford Fleming, who, as we all know, has been the originator and pioneer of the government-owned Pacific cable. For some years, people have thought that we should have on the Atlantic the system now existing between Australia and Canada, by which the Australian colonies are put in direct communication with America. The question arose whether there should not be an arrangement between the mother country and Canada and a new cable laid across the Atlantic. I, for one, and speaking only for myself, I viewed that project with great pleasure. But when I studied the question more in detail, and on following the discussions which took place at the various conferences in London, in which I was called upon to represent Canada, I found that, so far as the mother country was concerned, the number of shareholders in these cable companies was so great that strong objection would be taken to

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-CONTROL OF CABLE RATES.
speechtext: the government partaking in the work of laying a new cable. So, another scheme was devised to get a schedule of rates from the cable companies which would satisfy the public demand and satisfy the press. It was decided to propose for the acceptance of the cable companies that urgent messages should remain at the same rate as at present, namely, one shilling per word; for semi-urgent messages, 6d. a word, and a special rate for the press at 3d. a word. The actual rate for the press is 10 cents a word between England and Canada. That would be the tentative schedule of rates between the mother country and Canada. I need not dwell on the advantages such a rate would be to both countries from the imperial point of view and from the business point of view. Some years ago a blue-book was published by order of the House dealing fully with the subject, and the House will remember the correspondence which was laid on the table when Sir Wm. Mulock was Postmaster General.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is thinking of the Pacific end, I am speaking of the Atlantic side. On the Pacific side, it is true that we are partners with Australia, Great Britain and New Zealand in a Pacific cable, the rates for which were established by the Pacific Cable Board on which Canada is represented by Lord Strathcona. The business of the Pacific Cable Board haS not been a very prosperous one, but it is due to the unfair competition of the Eastern telegraph system. However, that question is too broad to be discussed here this evening. My hon. friend is right in stating that the Pacific Cable Board has not registered a surplus every year, but the Pacific Cable Board is paying expenses, and I think is putting aside something every year towards the payment of the whole system. Now to come back to the Atlantic end of this system, I have given the result of my investigations in England, and my discussions with the Postmaster General. I may say, however, that the establishment of a Pacific cable has had for effect to make a sensible reduction in the rates in the far east, it has had the effect to reduce conJ siderably the rates on all messages coming from Australia to Europe.
Mr. ARMSTRONG'. What reduction does the minister expect would be brought about by the present measure?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-CONTROL OF CABLE RATES.
speechtext:
I have discussed the matter with the Postmaster General in England, Mr. Buxton, and 1 agreed to introduce the present legislation to bring the cable companies under the authority of the

Railway Board, as the telegraph, telephone and railway companies are under the jurisdiction of that board to-day.
I expect that by concurrent legislation passed in England and Canada, we can bring the cable companies to establish a schedule of rates which, for urgent messages, will be the same as they are today, one shilling per word; for ,semi-urgent messages, or deferred messages, 6d. a word, and for press rates, 3d. a word. That is the object I have in view. Now there are two Bills before the House (No. 104) and (No. 105), and they must be read together. The object of the first Bill is to bring the cable companies operating between Great Britain and Canada, and all other cable companies touching Canadian territory, under the control of the Railway Commission. Another object is to bring cable companies operating in conjunction with telegraph companies under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board as regards rates. Traffic arrangements also would be subject to the jurisdiction of the board, just as in the case of railway, telephone and telegraph companies. They will have to submit their tariffs and tolls for the approval of the board within a period of four months after this Bill becomes law. The amendment proposed in the next Bill is to control the sending of telegrams. Under the proposed system, the telegraph companies will send first the urgent messages, then the deferred messages. There are five companies doing a cable business between Great Britain, Canada and the United States, namely, the Anglo-American, the Direct United States, La Compagnie Francaise, the Western Union and the Commercial Gfcible. The two first are British companies, the third is French, and thq last two belong to the United States. The Anglo-American has laid eight cables across the Atlantic, four of which have passed out of use, The Direct United States has one line, the French company one, the Western Union two, and the Commercial Cable five lines. All of these lines, seventeen in number, touch points in Canada. Of these thirteen are in service. The Anglo-American, the Direct United States, the French, and the Western Union companies have a pooling arrangement between them. They are allied with the Western Union, and the Great Northwestern companies for the transaction of their land business in Canada, and the United States. The Commercial Cable does not belong to the pool. Its land business is carried on by the Canadian Pacific Telegraph lines in Canada, and by the Postal Telegraph in the United States. I anticipate that we can come to a satisfactory arrangement with the cable companies by which a fair schedule of rates will be submitted to the Railway Board. On the whole I believe this legislation is highly desirable. It is the next best step, to my mind, to a government owned cable between Canada and Great Britain. As my hon. friends know the question was discussed at length at the last imperial press conference, and the sentiment was very strongly voiced that we should have cheaper telegraph and cable communications between Great Britain and Canada in order to disseminate news from the heart of the empire, and so bind more closely together the mother country and her colonies.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Paragraph 6a refers to time served in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. That force has a Pension Act similar to that of the permanent'force, and this is simply to facilitate an exchange from one corps to the other, so that if an officer who has served in the Mounted Police, should join the permanent force, the time he had served in the Mounted Police, and for which he had contributed would count in the militia. 6 (b) and the following paragraphs are intended to allow officers who served in the military service in South Africa or with the Constabulary in South Africa, or with the regiment which served at Halifax, to relieve the British garrisons there, and allow them to go to South Africa, or in the 200 men who served in the Yukon field force for two years, to count the time they served in that way in estimating their pension. Last, and perhaps more important that all others, it Is proposed now to allow any officer of the active militia who becomes an officer of the permanent force, and who serves in the permanent force ten years to count half the time he might have served with the active militia, not however, to exceed ten years. Thus if he had served thirty years in the active militia before becoming a permanent force officer, he could only count ten years, just
as if he had served twenty years. If he had served ten years he could count five years. This is thought to be desirable to encourage a better class of officers who have served in the active militia, and received - valuable experience there to come into the permanent force. It will be to the public advantage very often to take from the active militia an officer who has had the advantage of serving in that body. At present we cannot get these officers unless they are wealthy men to come into the permanent force late in life because there is no chance for them to get a pension. A man must have served twenty years in the permanent force in oTder to receive a pension. A man of forty-five who comes from the active militia into the permanent force cannot serve that length of time, so that officers of the active militia are not very desirous of going into the permanent force under existing conditions. We propose to improve the conditions in order to have the advantage of getting a few of the best officers of the active militia into the permanent force, and we think it will have a tendency to bring the two forces into better relations with each other. Such an officer coming into the permanent force from the active militia, we will say with a maximum of ten years credited to him, that is to say twenty years in the active militia, would pay, when the time comes that he would be entitled t-o a pension, his 5 per cent into the treasury for the whole of the ten years he had served in the active militia on the pay which he receives at the time he is pensioned. That is to say that 5 per cent would be deducted from his pension. That is upon the largest amount of pay of which he is in receipt, and it has been calculated that the loss to the treasury will be little if anything. In regard to this pension law as it applies to the permanent force, after ten years experience, it is just about self-sustaining, and there is not likely to be any very considerable deficiency even after this clause has been introduced into the law.
